Reading vector data¶

This tutorial reads vector datasets in two ways and plots the geometries.

open_vectors_data opens the file formats used by desktop GIS and GPS tools and returns a VectorDataset. open_cloud_native_vector_data opens cloud-native files, lakehouse tables, and GeoParquet profiles and returns a CloudNativeDataset. In both cases the active layer exposes the CRS, extent, fields, and feature count. to_dataframe() returns a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame when GeoPandas is installed. Close either dataset with a with block so the file handle is released.

The desktop-format files live in data/data_gdal. They are the GDAL sample files shipped with this repository. The cloud-native section writes small local examples, because those layouts are usually published as large objects on object storage. The tables below are where the same formats usually come from when you download real data.

Format Good sources
Shapefile Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com), US Census TIGER/Line, NYS GIS Clearinghouse (gis.ny.gov)
GeoJSON / GeoJSONSeq USGS Earthquake feeds (earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed), city open-data portals (Socrata/ArcGIS Hub "Download → GeoJSON"); GeoJSONSeq usually needs to be made with ogr2ogr -f GeoJSONSeq
KML / KMZ USGS Earthquake feeds, Google's KML samples (developers.google.com/kml), NOAA/NWS storm and warning products
GML Ordnance Survey (UK) OpenData, EU INSPIRE portals, WFS services (any WFS GetFeature returns GML)
GPX OpenStreetMap public GPS traces (openstreetmap.org/traces), Garmin/Strava exports, topografix.com sample files
CSV with X/Y or WKT USGS Earthquake CSV, NOAA station lists, EPA facility data (FRS), most data.gov tabular files
MapInfo TAB, MIF/MID data.gov.au and Geoscience Australia (still widely published there), GDAL autotest
DXF / DWG GDAL autotest, LibreDWG test files on GitHub, Autodesk sample files, municipal engineering/CAD portals
DGN GDAL autotest, state DOT CADD downloads (many DOTs use MicroStation), Bentley sample datasets
File Geodatabase (.gdb) USGS National Map (NHD, Watershed Boundary Dataset), TIGER/Line geodatabases, Esri sample data
SpatiaLite / SQLite Natural Earth (SQLite download), gaia-gis.it SpatiaLite sample DBs
FlatGeobuf flatgeobuf GitHub repo test/data (e.g., countries.fgb, UScounties.fgb)
OSM (.osm, .pbf) Geofabrik (download.geofabrik.de) for country and state .osm.pbf extracts, BBBike city extracts, the "Export" button on openstreetmap.org or the Overpass API for small .osm XML

Cloud-native files, lakehouse tables, and related layouts use open_cloud_native_vector_data. GeoParquet is the better choice for analytics on selected columns. FlatGeobuf is the better choice for a spatial lookup that returns whole features. PMTiles holds tiles for web display, not analysis-ready features. COPC is the point-cloud equivalent of those layouts.

Layout Good sources
GeoParquet Overture Maps releases, Microsoft Planetary Computer, national field-boundary datasets published as fiboa
GeoArrow In-memory exchange between GeoPandas, DuckDB, Sedona, and other Arrow tools; on disk as Feather or Arrow IPC
FlatGeobuf Source Cooperative and other static HTTP hosts; the client range-requests the features inside a bounding box
PMTiles Protomaps and Source Cooperative; one file replaces MBTiles and a tile server
GeoPackage QGIS exchange files and Natural Earth; not cloud-native, though GDAL can read a remote .gpkg
COPC USGS 3DEP and other LAZ octrees published for range-request access
Apache Iceberg Lakehouse tables; v3 adds native geometry and geography types on top of Parquet
Delta Lake Databricks and Sedona tables; geometry is stored as WKB
H3 / S2 Aggregated point tables that store a cell id instead of, or beside, a geometry

Setup¶

The next cell puts the repository root on the import path, points DATA at the sample directory, and defines three helpers:

  • list_layers prints one row per layer.
  • read_vector opens a desktop format with open_vectors_data, prints layer properties, shows a short attribute table, and draws the geometries.
  • read_cloud does the same for a cloud-native layout, and also prints the schema profile, reader, and spatial index.
In [1]:
%matplotlib inline

import sys
import tempfile
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from osgeo import gdal
from shapely.geometry.base import BaseGeometry

ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve()
if not (ROOT / "geolattice").is_dir():
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from geolattice.vector import (
    open_cloud_native_vector_data,
    open_vectors_data,
    supported_cloud_native_formats,
    supported_formats,
)
from geolattice.vector.open_vectors_data import (
    GEOM_POSSIBLE_NAMES,
    X_POSSIBLE_NAMES,
    Y_POSSIBLE_NAMES,
)

DATA = ROOT / "data" / "data_gdal"
assert DATA.is_dir(), DATA

gdal.PushErrorHandler("CPLQuietErrorHandler")
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 48)
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)

plt.rcParams.update(
    {
        "figure.facecolor": "white",
        "axes.facecolor": "white",
        "axes.edgecolor": "#98A2B3",
        "axes.labelcolor": "#344054",
        "axes.titlecolor": "#101828",
        "xtick.color": "#475467",
        "ytick.color": "#475467",
        "font.size": 11,
    }
)

_PLOT_TYPES = {
    "Polygon",
    "MultiPolygon",
    "LineString",
    "MultiLineString",
    "LinearRing",
    "Point",
    "MultiPoint",
}
RESULTS = []


def _resolve(relative):
    path = Path(relative)
    if path.exists():
        return path
    return DATA / relative


def _file_label(path):
    path = Path(path)
    try:
        return str(path.resolve().relative_to(DATA.resolve()))
    except ValueError:
        return str(path)


def preview_table(frame, limit=5):
    view = frame.head(limit).copy()
    view.insert(
        1,
        "geom_type",
        view["geometry"].map(lambda geom: getattr(geom, "geom_type", None)),
    )
    keep = ["fid", "geom_type"]
    extras = [name for name in view.columns if name not in keep and name != "geometry"]
    return view[keep + extras[:6]]


def plot_frame(frame, title):
    def plottable(geom):
        return isinstance(geom, BaseGeometry) and not geom.is_empty and geom.geom_type in _PLOT_TYPES

    mask = frame["geometry"].map(plottable)
    plot_df = frame.loc[mask].copy()
    if plot_df.empty:
        print(f"No point, line, or polygon geometries to draw for {title}.")
        return 0

    import geopandas as gpd

    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(plot_df, geometry="geometry", crs=None)
    polygons = gdf[gdf.geom_type.isin(["Polygon", "MultiPolygon"])]
    lines = gdf[gdf.geom_type.isin(["LineString", "MultiLineString", "LinearRing"])]
    points = gdf[gdf.geom_type.isin(["Point", "MultiPoint"])]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.4))
    handles = []
    if len(polygons):
        polygons.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="#2A6F97", edgecolor="#012A4A", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.88)
        handles.append(
            Line2D(
                [0],
                [0],
                marker="s",
                linestyle="none",
                markerfacecolor="#2A6F97",
                markeredgecolor="#012A4A",
                markersize=9,
                label="polygon",
            )
        )
    if len(lines):
        lines.plot(ax=ax, color="#E36414", linewidth=1.6)
        handles.append(Line2D([0], [0], color="#E36414", linewidth=1.6, label="line"))
    if len(points):
        points.plot(ax=ax, color="#F4A261", markersize=42, edgecolor="#7A3E00", linewidth=0.4)
        handles.append(
            Line2D(
                [0],
                [0],
                marker="o",
                linestyle="none",
                markerfacecolor="#F4A261",
                markeredgecolor="#7A3E00",
                markersize=8,
                label="point",
            )
        )

    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
    span_x = maxx - minx
    span_y = maxy - miny
    pad_x = span_x * 0.08 if span_x else max(abs(minx) * 0.02, 1.0)
    pad_y = span_y * 0.08 if span_y else max(abs(miny) * 0.02, 1.0)
    ax.set_xlim(minx - pad_x, maxx + pad_x)
    ax.set_ylim(miny - pad_y, maxy + pad_y)
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
    ax.ticklabel_format(useOffset=False, style="plain")
    ax.grid(True, linewidth=0.4, color="#E4E7EC")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=12, pad=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
    ax.set_ylabel("y")
    if len(handles) > 1:
        ax.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, loc="best")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    return len(gdf)


def geometry_bounds(frame):
    boxes = []
    for geom in frame["geometry"]:
        if isinstance(geom, BaseGeometry) and not geom.is_empty:
            boxes.append(geom.bounds)
    if not boxes:
        return None
    return (
        min(box[0] for box in boxes),
        min(box[1] for box in boxes),
        max(box[2] for box in boxes),
        max(box[3] for box in boxes),
    )


def list_layers(relative):
    path = _resolve(relative)
    with open_vectors_data(path) as dataset:
        print(f"{dataset.format_name}  |  driver {dataset.driver}  |  {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        rows = []
        for layer in dataset.layers:
            rows.append(
                {
                    "layer": layer.name,
                    "geometry_type": layer.geometry_type,
                    "features": layer.feature_count,
                    "crs": None if layer.crs is None else str(layer.crs),
                    "fields": len(layer.fields),
                }
            )
        display(pd.DataFrame(rows))


def read_vector(relative, layer=None, title=None, plot=True, limit=None):
    path = _resolve(relative)
    label = title or path.name
    with open_vectors_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset:
        active = dataset.layer
        frame = active.to_dataframe(limit=limit)
        read_bounds = geometry_bounds(frame)
        print(f"File:             {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        print(f"Format:           {dataset.format_name}")
        print(f"Driver:           {dataset.driver}")
        print(f"Layer count:      {dataset.layer_count}")
        print(f"Layer names:      {dataset.layer_names}")
        print(f"Active layer:     {active.name}")
        print(f"Geometry type:    {active.geometry_type}")
        print(f"Geometry source:  {active.geometry_source}")
        print(f"Feature count:    {active.feature_count}")
        print(f"Features read:    {len(frame)}")
        print(f"CRS:              {active.crs}")
        print(f"Bounds:           {read_bounds if read_bounds is not None else active.bounds}")
        print("Fields:")
        for field in active.fields:
            width = f", width={field.width}" if field.width else ""
            print(f"  - {field.name} ({field.type_name}{width})")
        if dataset.warnings:
            print("Sidecar notes:")
            for note in dataset.warnings:
                print(f"  - {note}")
        display(preview_table(frame))
        if plot:
            plot_frame(frame, label)
        feature_count = active.feature_count if active.feature_count is not None else len(frame)
        RESULTS.append(
            {
                "file": _file_label(dataset.path),
                "format": dataset.format_name,
                "driver": dataset.driver,
                "layer": active.name,
                "features": feature_count,
                "crs": None if active.crs is None else str(active.crs),
                "status": "opened",
            }
        )
        return None



def read_cloud(
    relative,
    layer=None,
    title=None,
    plot=True,
    limit=None,
    bbox=None,
    columns=None,
    where=None,
):
    """Open one cloud-native layout and record what the reader reported."""
    path = _resolve(relative)
    label = title or path.name
    print(f"\n{'=' * 72}\n{label}\n{'=' * 72}")
    with open_cloud_native_vector_data(path, layer=layer) as dataset:
        active = dataset.layer
        frame = active.to_dataframe()
        if limit is not None:
            frame = frame.head(limit)
        print(f"File:              {_file_label(dataset.path)}")
        print(f"Format:            {dataset.format_name} ({dataset.format_id})")
        print(f"Schema:            {dataset.schema_name or '—'}")
        print(f"Reader:            {dataset.reader}")
        print(f"Spatial access:    {dataset.spatial_access}")
        print(f"Spatial index:     {dataset.spatial_index or '—'}")
        print(f"Geometry encoding: {dataset.geometry_encoding or '—'}")
        print(f"Layers:            {dataset.layer_count}")
        print(f"Active layer:      {active.name}")
        print(f"Features:          {active.feature_count}")
        print(f"CRS:               {active.crs}")
        extent = active.bounds if active.bounds is not None else active.compute_bounds()
        print(f"Extent:            {None if extent is None else extent.to_tuple()}")
        print("Fields:")
        for field in active.fields:
            print(f"  - {field.name} ({field.type_name})")
        if dataset.warnings:
            print("Notes:")
            for note in dataset.warnings:
                print(f"  - {note}")
        shown = frame
        if bbox is not None or columns is not None or where is not None:
            shown = active.to_dataframe(bbox=bbox, columns=columns, where=where, limit=limit)
            print(f"Filtered rows:     {len(shown)}")
        display(preview_table(shown))
        if plot:
            plot_frame(shown, label)
        feature_count = active.feature_count if active.feature_count is not None else len(frame)
        RESULTS.append(
            {
                "file": _file_label(dataset.path),
                "format": dataset.format_name,
                "driver": dataset.reader,
                "layer": active.name,
                "features": feature_count,
                "crs": None if active.crs is None else str(active.crs),
                "status": "opened",
            }
        )
    return None

Drivers in this GDAL build¶

supported_formats() lists every file type the desktop reader knows about and whether this GDAL build includes a driver for it. The walkthrough below follows the table in the introduction. GeoPackage and spreadsheets are in this list as well; they use the same open_vectors_data call. The cloud-native section later uses supported_cloud_native_formats(), which reports a reader rather than a GDAL driver.

Shapefile¶

A shapefile is a small group of files that share one basename. .shp holds geometry, .shx is the index, and .dbf holds attributes. .prj stores the CRS and .cpg stores the DBF encoding. Natural Earth, TIGER/Line, and the NYS GIS Clearinghouse still publish this format.

poly.shp is the classic GDAL polygon sample. It is in British National Grid (EPSG:27700) and carries AREA, EAS_ID, and PRFEDEA.

GeoJSON¶

GeoJSON is a single JSON document: a Feature, a FeatureCollection, or a bare geometry. City open-data portals and the USGS earthquake feeds offer it as a download. Coordinates in a GeoJSON file are longitude, latitude (EPSG:4326) unless the file says otherwise.

geojson/grenada.geojson is one administrative polygon for Grenada, with names and ISO codes in the properties.

GeoJSON Sequence¶

GeoJSON Sequence (also called GeoJSON Text Sequences, or newline-delimited GeoJSON) stores one feature per line. The extensions here are .geojsonl and .geojsons. A download is often produced with ogr2ogr -f GeoJSONSeq.

geojsonseq/test.geojsonl has two points and a foo attribute. The same file is opened again later with open_cloud_native_vector_data, which streams one feature per line.

KML and KMZ¶

KML is the XML format used by Google Earth. A KMZ file is a zip archive with a KML document inside, usually named doc.kml. USGS earthquake feeds, Google's KML samples, and National Weather Service warning products are common sources.

kml/samples.kml is a Google sample document. Each folder becomes a layer, and those layers sit in different parts of the world, so they are drawn separately. This sample collection has no .kmz file. The last cell zips kml/placemark.kml into a temporary KMZ and opens that archive, which is the path open_vectors_data uses for KMZ.

GML¶

GML is the OGC XML encoding used by INSPIRE downloads, Ordnance Survey OpenData, and WFS GetFeature responses. A dataset can contain several layers, and the CRS is declared on the features or the envelope.

gml/gnis_pop_110.gml is a small WFS extract of populated places. Each feature is a point with a name and a population.

GPX¶

GPX is the GPS exchange format written by Garmin, Strava, and OpenStreetMap trace uploads. GDAL exposes five layers: waypoints, routes, tracks, route_points, and track_points. The sample below is a small GPX 1.1 file. Tracks and waypoints are the two layers with coordinates worth drawing.

CSV with X/Y or WKT¶

Delimited text becomes a vector layer when a column holds WKT, or when two columns hold X and Y (longitude and latitude, easting and northing). Earthquake CSV feeds, NOAA station lists, and many data.gov tables are published this way.

Column names the reader checks are printed below. wkt.csv uses a WKT column of polygons, so the geometry is built from that column. Pass x_possible_names and y_possible_names when a table uses a different pair, such as lon and lat.

MapInfo TAB and MIF/MID¶

MapInfo TAB is a binary workspace: .tab, .map, .dat (or .dbf), and .id. MIF/MID is the text interchange pair. .mif holds geometry and .mid holds attributes. Australian open data, including Geoscience Australia, still publishes both.

Opening a .mid path reads the sibling .mif. all_geoms.tab mixes points, lines, and polygons. small.mif is two polygons.

DXF and DWG¶

DXF is Autodesk's text drawing exchange. DWG is the binary drawing format. GDAL reads DXF with the DXF driver and DWG with the CAD driver (libopencad), which covers older DWG releases. Municipal CAD portals and engineering archives are the usual source.

dxf/assorted.dxf mixes lines and points in one entities layer. cad/line_r2000.dwg is a single R2000 line. A newer DWG that this CAD driver does not recognize is reported as an open error rather than an empty layer.

File Geodatabase¶

An Esri File Geodatabase is a directory whose name ends in .gdb. USGS National Map products (NHD, Watershed Boundary Dataset) and TIGER/Line geodatabases use it. OpenFileGDB reads the directory without the Esri FileGDB SDK.

openfilegdb/polygon_golden.gdb holds one multipolygon in EPSG:4326.

SpatiaLite and SQLite¶

SpatiaLite stores vectors inside a SQLite database. Natural Earth offers a SQLite download, and the Gaia-SINS site publishes sample databases. The SQLite driver reads SpatiaLite geometry when GDAL is built with SpatiaLite.

sqlite/poly_spatialite.sqlite is the same polygon set as poly.shp, stored as a SpatiaLite layer named poly.

FlatGeobuf¶

FlatGeobuf (.fgb) is a single binary file with a spatial index packed into the header, which makes it practical to read from cloud storage. The format's own test data, including country and county extracts, lives in the flatgeobuf repository.

testfgb/poly.fgb is again the GDAL polygon sample, in EPSG:27700. A later section opens this same file with open_cloud_native_vector_data and a bounding-box filter, which is the range-request path used for a remote .fgb.

OpenStreetMap¶

OSM XML (.osm) is what the openstreetmap.org export button and the Overpass API return for a small area. Protocolbuffer Binary Format (.osm.pbf) is the country and state extract from Geofabrik and BBBike. GDAL's OSM driver splits a file into points, lines, multilinestrings, multipolygons, and other_relations. Feature counts stay empty until the file is scanned, which is normal for this driver.

osm/test.osm is a tiny hand-written extract. osm/two_points.pbf is the same kind of data in PBF.

Cloud-native layouts¶

open_cloud_native_vector_data covers files that are meant to be read in pieces from object storage, plus the lakehouse tables and GeoParquet profiles built on the same idea. read_cloud prints the format, the schema profile when one is detected, the reader that did the work, and how a spatial lookup is served.

supported_cloud_native_formats() is the catalog. available is true when the reader this environment needs is installed. FlatGeobuf, PMTiles, GeoPackage, COPC, and GeoJSON Sequence run with the packages already used above. GeoParquet and GeoArrow need PyArrow. Lance and TileDB stay unavailable until those libraries are installed; the catalog still lists them.

In [28]:
CLOUD = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="geolattice_cloud_"))
print(f"Cloud-native examples: {CLOUD}")

cloud_catalog = pd.DataFrame(supported_cloud_native_formats())
cloud_catalog["extensions"] = cloud_catalog["extensions"].map(lambda names: ", ".join(names))
display(
    cloud_catalog[
        ["name", "family", "extensions", "spatial_access", "available"]
    ].rename(columns={"name": "format", "spatial_access": "spatial access"})
)

GeoParquet¶

GeoParquet stores features in a Parquet file and records the geometry column, encoding, bounding box, and CRS in a geo metadata key. A query can read a few columns instead of every attribute. fiboa, stac-geoparquet, and Overture Maps are schemas on top of that file: format_name stays GeoParquet and schema_name names the profile.

The cities file below is filtered twice: once with where on population, and once with a bounding box that also keeps only the name column. A where term has to name a column that is still loaded, so the attribute filter and the column projection are separate calls.

A binary geometry column without the geo key is still decoded as WKB, with a warning that the GeoParquet metadata is missing. A Parquet file that uses the 2025 GEOMETRY or GEOGRAPHY logical type, and has no geo key, is reported as Parquet GEOMETRY / GEOGRAPHY instead.

In [29]:
import json

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from shapely.geometry import Point
from shapely.wkb import dumps as dump_wkb


def write_geoparquet(path, columns, geo=None, metadata=None):
    arrays = []
    fields = []
    for name, values in columns.items():
        if isinstance(values[0], (bytes, bytearray)):
            arrays.append(pa.array(values, type=pa.binary()))
            fields.append(pa.field(name, pa.binary()))
        else:
            arrays.append(pa.array(values))
            fields.append(pa.field(name, arrays[-1].type))
    file_meta = {}
    if geo is not None:
        file_meta[b"geo"] = json.dumps(geo).encode("utf-8")
    if metadata:
        for key, value in metadata.items():
            file_meta[key.encode("utf-8")] = value.encode("utf-8")
    schema = pa.schema(fields, metadata=file_meta or None)
    pq.write_table(pa.table(dict(zip(columns, arrays)), schema=schema), path)


def point_geo(xs, ys):
    return {
        "version": "1.1.0",
        "primary_column": "geometry",
        "columns": {
            "geometry": {
                "encoding": "WKB",
                "geometry_types": ["Point"],
                "bbox": [min(xs), min(ys), max(xs), max(ys)],
                "crs": {"id": {"authority": "EPSG", "code": 4326}},
            }
        },
    }


xs = [0.0, 2.0, 4.0]
ys = [1.0, 3.0, 5.0]
write_geoparquet(
    CLOUD / "cities.parquet",
    {
        "name": ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"],
        "population": [10, 20, 30],
        "geometry": [dump_wkb(Point(x, y)) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)],
    },
    geo=point_geo(xs, ys),
)
read_cloud(CLOUD / "cities.parquet", title="GeoParquet — cities")
read_cloud(

)
read_cloud(

GeoArrow¶

GeoArrow is the in-memory form of the same geometry. On disk it is an Arrow IPC or Feather file whose geometry column carries an Arrow extension name such as geoarrow.wkb. Tools that already speak Arrow can pass the column without converting it to GeoJSON.

In [30]:
import pyarrow.feather as feather

arrow_schema = pa.schema(
    [
        pa.field("name", pa.string()),
        pa.field("geometry", pa.binary(), metadata={b"ARROW:extension:name": b"geoarrow.wkb"}),
    ]
)
arrow_table = pa.table(
    {"name": ["alpha", "beta"], "geometry": [dump_wkb(Point(8, 9)), dump_wkb(Point(1, 2))]},
    schema=arrow_schema,
)
feather.write_feather(arrow_table, CLOUD / "sites.feather")
read_cloud(CLOUD / "sites.feather", title="GeoArrow — Feather WKB")

FlatGeobuf range requests¶

The desktop section opened testfgb/poly.fgb through GDAL. The cloud-native reader uses the same driver and reports the packed Hilbert R-tree, which is what a remote .fgb uses for an HTTP range request. The bounding box below covers the north-east part of the sample, so the table is a subset of the ten polygons.

PMTiles¶

A PMTiles archive is one file of map tiles. A static host or an S3 bucket can serve it with HTTP range requests, which replaces a tile server. The tiles are for display. read_tile(z, x, y) returns the bytes of one tile. When the archive holds Mapbox Vector Tiles, the same file also yields features through GDAL.

This cell writes a two-zoom point archive with the PMTiles driver, then reads the features and the tile at zoom 0.

In [32]:
from osgeo import ogr, osr

pmtiles_path = CLOUD / "places.pmtiles"
pmtiles_srs = osr.SpatialReference()
pmtiles_srs.ImportFromEPSG(4326)
pmtiles_srs.SetAxisMappingStrategy(osr.OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER)
pmtiles_ds = ogr.GetDriverByName("PMTiles").CreateDataSource(str(pmtiles_path))
pmtiles_layer = pmtiles_ds.CreateLayer(
    "places", pmtiles_srs, ogr.wkbPoint, options=["MINZOOM=0", "MAXZOOM=2"]
)
pmtiles_layer.CreateField(ogr.FieldDefn("name", ogr.OFTString))
for label, x_coord, y_coord in (("alpha", 10.0, 20.0), ("beta", 12.0, 22.0)):
    feature = ogr.Feature(pmtiles_layer.GetLayerDefn())
    feature.SetField("name", label)
    geometry = ogr.Geometry(ogr.wkbPoint)
    geometry.AddPoint_2D(x_coord, y_coord)
    feature.SetGeometry(geometry)
    pmtiles_layer.CreateFeature(feature)
pmtiles_layer = None
pmtiles_ds = None

read_cloud(pmtiles_path, title="PMTiles — places")
with open_cloud_native_vector_data(pmtiles_path) as dataset:
    tile = dataset.read_tile(0, 0, 0)
    gzip_tile = tile.startswith(bytes([0x1F, 0x8B]))
    print(f"Tile 0/0/0: {len(tile)} bytes, gzip={gzip_tile}")
    print("Vector layer:", dataset.details["metadata"]["vector_layers"][0]["id"])

GeoPackage¶

GeoPackage is a SQLite database and the usual replacement for a shapefile. It is not cloud-native: a client generally downloads the file before reading it. GDAL can still open a remote .gpkg, and the cloud-native reader uses that driver so the call looks the same as GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf.

In [33]:
gpkg_path = CLOUD / "sites.gpkg"
gpkg_srs = osr.SpatialReference()
gpkg_srs.ImportFromEPSG(4326)
gpkg_srs.SetAxisMappingStrategy(osr.OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER)
gpkg_ds = ogr.GetDriverByName("GPKG").CreateDataSource(str(gpkg_path))
gpkg_layer = gpkg_ds.CreateLayer("sites", gpkg_srs, ogr.wkbPoint)
gpkg_layer.CreateField(ogr.FieldDefn("name", ogr.OFTString))
for label, x_coord, y_coord in (("alpha", 1.0, 2.0), ("beta", 3.0, 4.0)):
    feature = ogr.Feature(gpkg_layer.GetLayerDefn())
    feature.SetField("name", label)
    geometry = ogr.Geometry(ogr.wkbPoint)
    geometry.AddPoint_2D(x_coord, y_coord)
    feature.SetGeometry(geometry)
    gpkg_layer.CreateFeature(feature)
gpkg_layer = None
gpkg_ds = None
read_cloud(gpkg_path, layer="sites", title="GeoPackage — sites")

COPC¶

Cloud Optimized Point Cloud is a LAZ file whose header carries an octree. A client range-requests the voxels inside a bounding box instead of downloading the file. This example is an uncompressed point-format 6 file with one root voxel, so it can be read without a LAZ decompressor. A compressed .copc.laz needs laspy and lazrs; the header and hierarchy are still readable without them.

In [34]:
import struct

copc_path = CLOUD / "cloud.copc.laz"
points = [(1.0, 2.0, 3.0), (4.0, 6.0, 8.0)]
wkt = (
    'GEOGCS["WGS 84",DATUM["WGS_1984",SPHEROID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257223563]],'
    'PRIMEM["Greenwich",0],UNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433],AUTHORITY["EPSG","4326"]]'
).encode("ascii") + b"\x00"
scale = 0.001
point_blob = bytearray()
for x_coord, y_coord, z_coord in points:
    point_blob.extend(
        struct.pack(
            "<3iHBBBBhHd",
            int(round(x_coord / scale)),
            int(round(y_coord / scale)),
            int(round(z_coord / scale)),
            0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.0,
        )
    )
info_payload = struct.pack("<5dQQ2d11d", 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 50.0, 1.0, 0, 32, 0.0, 0.0, *([0.0] * 11))
vlr_copc = bytearray(54 + len(info_payload))
vlr_copc[2:6] = b"copc"
struct.pack_into("<HH", vlr_copc, 18, 1, len(info_payload))
vlr_copc[54:] = info_payload
vlr_wkt = bytearray(54 + len(wkt))
vlr_wkt[2:18] = b"LASF_Projection"
struct.pack_into("<HH", vlr_wkt, 18, 2112, len(wkt))
vlr_wkt[54:] = wkt
offset_points = 375 + len(vlr_copc) + len(vlr_wkt)
hier_offset = offset_points + len(point_blob)
struct.pack_into("<Q", vlr_copc, 54 + 40, hier_offset)
struct.pack_into("<Q", vlr_copc, 54 + 48, 32)
xs, ys, zs = zip(*points)
header = bytearray(375)
header[0:4] = b"LASF"
header[24] = 1
header[25] = 4
struct.pack_into("<H", header, 94, 375)
struct.pack_into("<I", header, 96, offset_points)
struct.pack_into("<I", header, 100, 2)
header[104] = 6
struct.pack_into("<H", header, 105, 30)
struct.pack_into("<3d", header, 131, scale, scale, scale)
struct.pack_into("<6d", header, 179, max(xs), min(xs), max(ys), min(ys), max(zs), min(zs))
struct.pack_into("<Q", header, 247, len(points))
hierarchy = struct.pack("<4iQii", 0, 0, 0, 0, offset_points, len(point_blob), len(points))
copc_path.write_bytes(bytes(header) + bytes(vlr_copc) + bytes(vlr_wkt) + bytes(point_blob) + hierarchy)

read_cloud(
    copc_path,
    title="COPC — two points",
    bbox=(0, 0, 2, 3),
    columns=["x", "y", "z"],
)
with open_cloud_native_vector_data(copc_path) as dataset:
    print("Octree nodes:", len(dataset.hierarchy))
    print("Spacing:", dataset.copc["spacing"])

Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg¶

Both are directories of Parquet files plus a transaction log. Iceberg v3 can declare a field as geometry or geography. Delta Lake has no geometry type, so the geometry column is WKB and the reader says so.

Without the deltalake or pyiceberg packages, these cells read a local table from the JSON log and the Parquet data files. A remote table needs the matching package.

In [35]:
delta_root = CLOUD / "places_delta"
delta_root.mkdir()
write_geoparquet(delta_root / "part-000.parquet", {"name": ["old"], "geometry": [dump_wkb(Point(1, 1))]})
write_geoparquet(
    delta_root / "part-001.parquet",
    {"name": ["new"], "geometry": [dump_wkb(Point(9, 8))]},
    geo=point_geo([9], [8]),
)
delta_schema = {
    "type": "struct",
    "fields": [
        {"name": "name", "type": "string", "nullable": True, "metadata": {}},
        {"name": "geometry", "type": "binary", "nullable": True, "metadata": {}},
    ],
}
delta_log = delta_root / "_delta_log"
delta_log.mkdir()


def delta_commit(number, actions):
    text = "".join(json.dumps(action) + "\n" for action in actions)
    (delta_log / f"{number:020d}.json").write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")


delta_commit(
    0,
    [
        {"protocol": {"minReaderVersion": 1, "minWriterVersion": 2}},
        {
            "metaData": {
                "id": "places",
                "format": {"provider": "parquet", "options": {}},
                "schemaString": json.dumps(delta_schema),
                "partitionColumns": [],
                "configuration": {},
                "createdTime": 1,
            }
        },
        {
            "add": {
                "path": "part-000.parquet",
                "partitionValues": {},
                "size": 1,
                "modificationTime": 1,
                "dataChange": True,
            }
        },
    ],
)
delta_commit(
    1,
    [
        {"remove": {"path": "part-000.parquet", "deletionTimestamp": 2, "dataChange": True}},
        {
            "add": {
                "path": "part-001.parquet",
                "partitionValues": {},
                "size": 1,
                "modificationTime": 2,
                "dataChange": True,
            }
        },
    ],
)
read_cloud(delta_root, title="Delta Lake — live file only")

iceberg_root = CLOUD / "places_iceberg"
(iceberg_root / "data").mkdir(parents=True)
(iceberg_root / "metadata").mkdir()
write_geoparquet(
    iceberg_root / "data" / "00000.parquet",
    {"name": ["alpha"], "geometry": [dump_wkb(Point(7, 11))]},
    geo=point_geo([7], [11]),
)
iceberg_metadata = {
    "format-version": 3,
    "table-uuid": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001",
    "location": str(iceberg_root),
    "current-schema-id": 0,
    "schemas": [
        {
            "schema-id": 0,
            "type": "struct",
            "fields": [
                {"id": 1, "name": "name", "required": False, "type": "string"},
                {"id": 2, "name": "geometry", "required": False, "type": "geometry"},
            ],
        }
    ],
    "current-snapshot-id": None,
    "snapshots": [],
}
(iceberg_root / "metadata" / "v3.metadata.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(iceberg_metadata), encoding="utf-8"
)
read_cloud(iceberg_root, title="Apache Iceberg v3 — geometry field")

H3 and S2 cell indexes¶

Some Parquet tables store an H3 or S2 cell id instead of a geometry. The reader recognizes column names such as h3_index and s2_token. The cell id stays in the attribute table. A polygon is built only when the h3 or s2sphere package is installed.

In [37]:
write_geoparquet(
    CLOUD / "hex.parquet",
    {"h3_index": ["8928308280fffff"], "count": [4]},
)
read_cloud(CLOUD / "hex.parquet", title="H3 — cell id column", plot=False)

The table collects every file this notebook opened, including the cloud-native examples. The driver column is the GDAL driver for desktop formats and the reader name (pyarrow, gdal, pmtiles+gdal, copc, delta-log, iceberg-metadata) for cloud-native layouts.
